extracted.intended_audience: writers/creators and fans of film/TV/comics/games interested in using or understanding credits-based humor (credits gags)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive catalogue of comedic devices that target or appear within opening/closing/title/credits sequences across media (film, TV, animation, comics, games, web). Explains common variants, examples, and how credits are played for humor, meta-commentary, or narrative effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broken credits / arguments over fixing them
rubrics_metrics.description: The credits getting "broken" and arguments over fixing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Play the credits sequence as if the mechanism has failed or the crew is arguing about how to present the credits; example: Monty Python's fake subtitles and successive 'sackings' escalate into nonsense. Use timing, restarting credits, or deliberately garbled visuals/colours to create escalating absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spoof credits (fake names, nonsensical or ridiculous roles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spoof credits, such as fake names, nonsensical or ridiculous roles, or fictional characters supposedly working behind the scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace real personnel with joke job titles or fictional participants; common in comics and films (e.g., Stan Lee-era Marvel, comedy films crediting invented roles). Works well when the gag relates to the story theme (e.g., Hollywood issue: writer labelled 'screenwriter', artist 'director').

rubrics_metrics.name: Referencing things within the credits (self-deprecating / meta references)
rubrics_metrics.description: Referencing things within the credits, sometimes in a self-deprecating manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the credits comment on themselves or the production (mocking mistakes, calling out poor quality), or include meta-notes. Examples include mock apologies in subtitles or credits that explicitly shame or joke about the production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Running fake credits before the end (fake-out credits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Running fake credits before the end of the show, only to continue later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a premature credit roll as a bait-and-switch — can be used to fake 'end' or to produce a gag when the action resumes. Examples: Andy Kaufman style recuts, films that show 'The End' early then continue, and episodes where credits roll then are interrupted.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-person-many-roles (homemade production gag)
rubrics_metrics.description: Homemade productions made by one person list job after job after job; with the same person's name next to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In low-budget or solo projects, exaggerate multi-tasking by crediting the same name repeatedly for dozens of roles to comedic effect; common in fan works, ROM hacks, and personal projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke legal disclaimers / parody warnings
rubrics_metrics.description: Joke legal disclaimers. Variants on 'No Animals Were Harmed' or 'This Is a Work of Fiction' and other faux-legal text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subvert the dry legalese with absurd or in-character text (e.g., Fight Club's incendiary 'warning' text, parody piracy warnings read in-character). Can be voiced-over or shown as rolling text; be mindful of tone when touching sensitive topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply gag to the title or studio logos
rubrics_metrics.description: This is not just limited to the actual credits though, a film/series title gets this treatment too.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manipulate the title sequence or studio logos (parodies, rewordings, animations) to produce the gag — e.g., parodying Bewitched opening in Nyaruko, or swapping studio names to in-universe variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credits listing characters as production staff / in-character credits
rubrics_metrics.description: The credits include characters from the show among the production staff or credit characters as playing themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credit fictional characters as if they were real crew (e.g., Haruhi crediting 'The Ultra Director Haruhi Suzumiya', or shows crediting all characters as themselves). Useful for breaking the fourth wall or extending character-based humor into the meta-space of production.

rubrics_metrics.name: In-character voiceovers/paraphrases for standard warnings
rubrics_metrics.description: In-character voiceovers from cast to accompany standard warnings (e.g., FBI/piracy warnings paraphrased in-character).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have characters read/interpret legal/piracy or safety warnings in a way consistent with their personalities — used in anime dubs like Full Metal Panic! and Ranma ½ dubs. Good for keeping brand voice even in legal bits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credits that convey additional narrative or foreshadowing
rubrics_metrics.description: Credits that include conversations or text that refer to events in the story or future relationship developments (e.g., Line conversations in closing credits, credits referencing future events).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use credit text/overlay to add story beats, epilogues, or teasers (e.g., Tsuki ga Kirei's messaging sequence). This turns credits into an extension of storytelling rather than pure metadata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual/linguistic tricks in names (anagrams, backwards names, letter substitutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Credits using anagrams, backward names, or letter substitution as jokes (e.g., Sdrawkcab Alias, Makken/Reo Kaminaga scramble, S1m0ne replacing I/O).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ wordplay on names and titles to hide a gag or hint at an in-joke. Works best when attentive viewers can spot the transformation (rearranged letters, reversed names, substitutions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Credits used to pad or extend runtime (budget-driven long credits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using long, humorous credits to extend runtime when the film/show is too short or under budget.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write an intentionally long, escalating gag-credit sequence to fill time (Monty Python examples). Can double as meta-commentary (e.g., listing ridiculous credits because 'we ran out of money').

rubrics_metrics.name: Credits that spoil or reveal plot/cameo intentionally
rubrics_metrics.description: Credits that reveal a character/appearance before they appear (spoiler-credit) or play with audience expectation by crediting someone who then later appears in a stinger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use carefully: pre-crediting a character can be used to set up a stinger or to mislead/spoof expectations (Resident Evil: Jill Valentine credited before her appearance; Equestria Girls credit spoiling Spike). Consider audience reaction to spoilers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credits as performance (characters perform during/over credits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters/actors perform (sing/dance/act) alongside the credits, integrating the credits into an on-screen performance (e.g., Miyakawa sisters performing credits theme, VeggieTales pirates interrupting credits to sing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage an in-world performance that runs alongside the credits to create musical or visual comedy. Align song/bit to the film's tone or deliberately contrast it for humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit-box gags tied to issue/theme (thematic job renaming)
rubrics_metrics.description: Changing job titles or credits to items related to the issue/story (e.g., 'Hollywood issue' where positions are renamed to fit theme).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rename credits to reflect setting or plot (e.g., a jail-set issue giving jobs like 'warden'), reinforcing the issue's theme while generating laughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-commentary and direct address to audience in credits
rubrics_metrics.description: Credits that address or mock the audience or reading habits (e.g., Fight Club's warning that chides readers of fine print, Mary Poppins' eye-chart gag).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the credits to make jokes directed at those who read credits or to comment on viewing behavior. Can be biting or affectionate — match tone to audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interactive/mini-game credits in games (player can interact with credits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Credits that are interactive (mouse-over names for points, play mechanics running behind credits, mini-games during/after credits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage game mechanics to make credits part of gameplay (e.g., Punch-Out!! mini-game during credits, games that require actions while credits roll). Ensure accessibility: consider players who want to skip.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalized / signature credit segments (production babies, themed retitling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Personalized segments in credits (e.g., 'Production Babies' retitled to fit a film's motif; custom mosaics or tributes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt standard credit traditions (like production babies) to the film's theme for a resonant, humorous, or heartfelt touch (examples: Soul, Elio retitlings, Coco ofrenda mosaic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Credits that mock real people/positions or use parody honorifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Over-the-top, flattering, or insulting embellishments on names/positions (e.g., 'Spectacular Stan Lee', 'Master of the Macabre', Irving Forbush jokes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exaggerated honorifics or self-deprecating insults to lampoon industry conventions; works well in-house when creators are in on the joke. Avoid targeted defamation or mean-spirited real-world attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credits interrupted by stingers or extra scenes (stinger after or during credits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Credits sequences that are cut off by a stinger or that conceal additional content until after or during the credits (e.g., credits cut to a test pattern then continue; stinger showing a character after credits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interruption or hidden scenes to reward viewers who stay through credits (Resident Evil stinger, films promising stingers after credits). Timing and payoff are key: the stinger should justify the tease.
